title: Why the Museum Shortened Its Labels
passage:
A science museum was preparing a new exhibition about oceans. Curators had spent two years working with researchers, and they wanted visitors to understand the complexity of currents, ecosystems, fishing, climate, and plastic pollution. The first draft of the exhibition labels was detailed and accurate. Some wall panels contained more than five hundred words. During an early test, however, visitors rarely finished reading them.

The curators faced a familiar fear: shortening the text might oversimplify the science. One researcher argued that if important conditions and uncertainties were removed, visitors could leave with a misleading impression. A designer responded that information no one reads cannot communicate complexity either. The team decided not to choose between ‘long and accurate’ and ‘short and shallow.’ Instead, they tested layers of information.

The main labels were reduced to about one hundred words and focused on a single question. Beside them, smaller panels offered additional evidence, definitions, and exceptions. QR codes linked to interviews with scientists and full data sources. Objects and interactive displays carried their own short explanations. The idea was that every visitor would receive a clear core message, while those who wanted more could continue deeper.

The museum tested the new design with volunteers. More people read the main labels to the end. Yet another problem appeared: some visitors assumed the short statement was the entire scientific conclusion and did not notice the deeper panels. The design team changed headings from generic words such as ‘More Information’ to specific invitations such as ‘Why scientists are still uncertain’ or ‘What changed after 1990?’ Those headings made the next layer feel connected to a question rather than optional decoration.

Researchers also reviewed the shortened labels line by line. In several cases, simple wording accidentally removed an important limitation. For example, one draft said that warmer seas reduce fish populations. The researcher explained that the effect differs by species and region; some populations may move rather than simply decline. The final label said that warming can change where fish live and how many are found in particular areas. This remained understandable while avoiding a false universal claim.

After the exhibition opened, the museum observed visitors without tracking individuals. Most spent more time with the displays than in the original test. A minority used the QR codes, but many read at least one secondary panel. Teachers reported that the layered structure made it easier to assign different tasks to students with different levels of background knowledge.

The museum did not conclude that all labels should be short. Some historical objects required longer context, and certain visitors preferred detailed text. The lesson was about information architecture rather than word count alone. Complexity can be preserved by organizing it so readers know where to enter and how to continue.

The curators eventually described their task as building a staircase. The first step had to be low enough for most visitors to climb, but the staircase should not end there. A museum fails if it turns research into slogans, yet it also fails if accuracy is locked inside text so dense that almost nobody engages with it. The exhibition worked best when clarity was treated not as the enemy of complexity, but as the route into it.
translation:
科学博物館は海をテーマにした展示を準備し、海流、生態系、漁業、気候、プラスチック汚染の複雑さを正確に伝えようとしていました。最初の解説文は詳しく、一部は五百語を超えましたが、試験ではほとんどの来館者が最後まで読みませんでした。

文章を短くすれば科学を単純化しすぎるという不安がありました。一方で、誰も読まない情報では複雑さも伝わりません。そこで『長く正確』か『短く浅い』かの二択ではなく、情報を段階化しました。

主要ラベルは約百語にし、一つの問いに集中させました。その横に証拠、定義、例外を示す補助パネルを置き、QRコードから研究者のインタビューやデータへ進めるようにしました。全員が核となる説明を受け取り、興味があれば深く進める構造です。

試験では主要ラベルを最後まで読む人が増えましたが、短い説明だけが科学的結論のすべてだと思う人もいました。そこで『追加情報』のような曖昧な見出しをやめ、『なぜ科学者はまだ確信できないのか』『1990年以降何が変わったか』のような具体的な問いに変えました。

研究者は短文化によって重要な条件が消えていないか確認しました。例えば『海が暖まると魚が減る』では一般化しすぎるため、『温暖化によって魚の生息場所や地域ごとの数が変わることがある』と修正しました。

開館後、展示に費やす時間は増え、QRコード利用は少数でも、補助パネルを読む人は多くいました。教師からは、生徒の背景知識に応じて課題を変えやすいという評価もありました。

結論は『すべて短く』ではありません。重要なのは語数より情報の設計です。複雑さを残しつつ、どこから入り、どう深めるかを読者に示すことができます。博物館はこれを階段にたとえました。最初の段は低くても、そこで終わってはいけません。明快さは複雑さの敵ではなく、そこへ入るための道になり得るのです。
